rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Stress (σ = F/A) and strain (ε = Δl/l) describe how solids respond to deforming forces. Within the elastic limit, σ = Eε (Hooke's law). Elastic bodies recover their shape; plastic bodies deform permanently. The stress–strain curve shows the proportional limit, elastic limit, yield point, ultimate strength and fracture — ductile materials deform plastically first, brittle materials shatter suddenly.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Stress: σ = F/A (N/m² or Pa)
Strain: ε = Δl/l (dimensionless; ε_V = ΔV/V, shear ε = θ)
Hooke's law in stress–strain form: σ = Eε

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Stress-Strain vs Force-Extension:** Stress-strain curves are material properties (independent of geometry), while force-extension curves depend on the specific sample's dimensions. $E = \sigma/\varepsilon$ is a material constant; $k = F/x$ depends on length and cross-section.  ·  **Linear Region Constraint:** The linear proportionality $\sigma = E\varepsilon$ (Hooke's law) holds *only* up to the proportional limit. Beyond this, the curve is non-linear even before the elastic limit (where full recovery still occurs). The elastic limit and proportional limit are close but distinct.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Strain is dimensionless — never attach units.  ·  Stress and pressure share the N/m² unit but are different concepts (internal vs external).

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Stress: A 1000 N force on a 5 cm² bar gives σ = 1000/(5×10⁻⁴) = 2×10⁶ Pa.  ·  Strain: A wire stretched from 2.00 m to 2.01 m has ε = 0.01/2 = 5×10⁻³.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: ❌ 'Stress and pressure are the same.' ✅ Both have units N/m², but stress is the INTERNAL resisting force per unit area produced in a body, while pressure is an EXTERNAL force per unit area applied by a fluid.  ·  ❌ 'Strain has units.' ✅ Strain is dimensionless — it is a ratio of lengths (or volumes/angles). This is essential for dimensional analysis.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Calculate stress, strain and Young's modulus for a loaded wire with correct unit conversions.  ·  Label all six regions on a mild steel stress–strain curve.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Remember: strain has NO units — a quick sanity check for MCQs.  ·  To find E: rearrange to E = Fl/(AΔl) — compute σ then divide by ε.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: A steel rod of length 3 m and area 2 cm² is stretched by a 6000 N force. Given E = 2×10¹¹ N/m², find stress, strain and extension.  ·  A rubber band of original length 10 cm stretches to 12 cm. Find the strain and the percentage elongation.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Stress and strain numericals are a guaranteed exam topic — practice unit conversions (mm² → m²).  ·  Labeling the stress–strain curve and identifying regions carries direct marks.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Stress σ = F/A is the internal force per unit area resisting deformation.  ·  Strain ε = Δl/l is the dimensionless fractional deformation.  ·  Hooke's law: σ = Eε inside the elastic limit.  ·  Elasticity recovers shape; plasticity causes permanent deformation.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Stress is force per unit area; strain is fractional deformation (dimensionless).  ·  Elasticity = recovery of shape when the force is removed; plasticity = permanent deformation.  ·  Stress is proportional to strain only within the elastic limit (Hooke's law, σ = Eε).  ·  The stress–strain curve has six regions: proportional, elastic, yield, plastic, ultimate, fracture.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Stress and strain were first quantified by Robert Hooke and later generalised by Thomas Young, after whom Young's modulus is named.  ·  The area under the stress–strain curve equals the energy absorbed per unit volume (toughness) — important for crash safety design.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: A column of area 0.25 m² supports a weight of 2.5×10⁵ N. Find the compressive stress.  ·  A mild steel wire of area 1 mm² breaks when the stress reaches 4×10⁸ Pa. Find the breaking (maximum) load.  ·  A body under 10⁵ Pa pressure suffers a volume strain of 2×10⁻⁴. Find its bulk modulus.

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: Young's modulus problems (extension of a wire) appear almost every year.  ·  Bulk modulus and shear modulus are often asked as short-answer comparisons.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Young's modulus: σ = 1.96×10⁸ Pa, ε = 9.8×10⁻⁴ → E = 2×10¹¹ N/m² (steel).  ·  Shear: A force parallel to the top face of a cube displaces it — shear stress τ = F/A, shear strain θ.

rows.text: The SI unit of stress is: → B  ·  Strain is: → B

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Stress (σ):** the internal resisting force per unit area set up in a body when external forces are applied: σ = F/A. Empirical units are N/m² or Pa (pascal). Normal stress = force perpendicular to the area (tension/compression); shear stress = force parallel to the area.  ·  **Strain (ε):** the fractional deformation produced: strain = change in dimension / original dimension. It is dimensionless. Linear strain = Δl/l, shear strain = θ (angle of shear), volumetric strain = ΔV/V.  ·  **Elasticity and plasticity:** elasticity is the property of a body to regain its original shape and size when the deforming force is removed. Plasticity is the property of remaining permanently deformed after the deforming force is removed. Bodies are elastic below the elastic limit and plastic beyond it.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Moduli: E (Young), G (shear), B (bulk) each relate a stress to its corresponding strain.  ·  Young's modulus: E = (F/A)/(Δl/l) = Fl/(AΔl)  ·  Bulk modulus: B = −P/(ΔV/V); Shear modulus: G = τ/θ

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Ductile vs Brittle Failure Mode:** Ductile materials have a significant plastic region (yield, strain hardening, necking) and fracture after large deformation. Brittle materials fracture near the elastic limit with little/no plastic deformation — no warning before failure.  ·  Ductile materials deform plastically before breaking; brittle ones break suddenly near the elastic limit.  ·  ❌ 'Elasticity means materials are always elastic.' ✅ Every material is elastic only up to its elastic limit; beyond it, plastic deformation occurs.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ 'Stress equals force.' ✅ Stress is force PER unit area (σ = F/A). Doubling the area halves the stress for the same force.  ·  ❌ 'The stress–strain graph is a straight line everywhere.' ✅ Only up to the proportional limit. After that it curves at the yield point and beyond.  ·  ❌ 'A ductile material breaks near the elastic limit.' ✅ DUCTILE materials deform plastically and stretch before fracturing; brittle materials break with little warning near the elastic limit.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Volume: Pressure P on a sphere → B = −P/(ΔV/V). For water, B ≈ 2.2×10⁹ Pa.  ·  The elastic limit is the maximum stress from which the body still recovers fully.  ·  For safety design, working stress is kept well below the yield/ultimate stress (safety factor).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: NEB frequently asks to label the stress–strain curve and to calculate E from a numerical.  ·  Always distinguish stress (F/A) from strain (Δl/l) — one has units, one is dimensionless.  ·  The elastic limit is the boundary between recoverable (elastic) and permanent (plastic) deformation.
